report:
Your skepticism is correct: the claim that boiled garlic water cures COVID-19 is false.

This claim originated early in the pandemic (around January–February 2020) and spread widely on social media, particularly in messages misattributed to sources in China, Japan, or health authorities. Multiple independent fact-checking organizations investigated and debunked it. FactCheck.org found the claim traces to unverified viral posts claiming a bowl of freshly boiled garlic water could cure the virus overnight—there is no evidence supporting this (https://www.factcheck.org/2020/02/fake-coronavirus-cures-part-2-garlic-isnt-a-cure/). AFP Fact Check similarly reported that health professionals confirmed as early as February 2020 that no evidence exists for garlic water as an effective COVID-19 treatment (https://factcheck.afp.com/health-experts-refute-false-claims-drinking-boiled-garlic-water-cures-novel-coronavirus). Africa Check reached the same conclusion, noting the World Health Organization has stated there is no approved vaccine, drug, or treatment that cures COVID-19—garlic included (https://africacheck.org/fact-checks/meta-programme-fact-checks/no-garlic-doesnt-cure-coronavirus-get-covid-19-facts-only). The WHO's own "Mythbusters" resource reinforces that no home remedy, including garlic preparations, has been validated as a COVID-19 cure (https://www.who.int/emergencies/diseases/novel-coronavirus-2019/advice-for-public/myth-busters).

While laboratory research suggests garlic contains organosulfur compounds with some general antiviral and immune-modulating properties, this is distinct from claiming garlic water cures an active COVID-19 infection in humans—no clinical trials have demonstrated such an effect, and health authorities have consistently rejected the specific "cure" claim.

**Conclusion:** The claim is false. It was a pandemic-era myth debunked by multiple fact-checkers and contradicted by WHO guidance, despite garlic having some general antiviral properties unrelated to curing COVID-19.
